newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel backs away from severing PLO talks.
newsitem.headline: Israel backs away from severing PLO talks.

text.p: Israel backed away from severing negotiations with the PLO on Sunday while accusing it of fomenting unrest alongside sanctioning guerrilla attacks.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he would not suspend peace talks with the Palestinian Authority over a Moslem suicide bomb attack that killed three women in Tel Aviv on Friday.

"Well, I'm not suspending talks because our people are meeting with their people but the first item on the agenda is the fulfillment of the Palestinian obligation to fight terrorism. They have to start complying with that or else we can't move," Netanyahu told CNN cable television.
Netanyahu was responding to one of his interviewers who asked him if he would, as one of his aides had hinted earlier in the day, halt political talks.

Palestinian Authority negotiator Saeb Erekat rejected Netanyahu's criticism, telling CNN the Authority had fought extremists in its society but Netanyahu's beginning a new settlement and other actions had encouraged militants.
"I think if there is one person would would look in the mirror tonight and see the blood...if Mr Netanyahu would look in the mirror, he will see the real responsibility," Erekat said.

The Israeli prime minister appeared after meeting for several hours with key government ministers on a reaction to the bombing, which a caller to Israeli police claimed was the responsibility of the militant group Hamas.

A statement released after the meeting said: "The government of Israel demands from the Palestinian Authority that it uphold its commitments to fight terror and violence, as a necessary step, to furthering the political process."

It demanded, but did not specifically make a condition, that the Authority increase security cooperation; prevent incitement against Israel; fight guerrilla organisations including their infrastructures; arrest, try and punish "terrorists"; deal with Israel's extradition requests; and confiscate illegal weapons.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, asked on a CBS network programme "Face the Nation" if Arafat had given a "green light" for violence, said: "There is clearly perception of the green light but no concrete evidence."
Albright said Arafat had to do more to stop violence.

"There have been efforts on his part, 100 percent efforts, to stop the violence and the terrorism, but the result has not been 100 percent," she said. "He has condemned the violent acts, but there needs to be some improvement."
Israel's military intelligence chief Major General Moshe Yaalon said at a news conference that the Authority was conditioning cooperation in fighting "terror" on a change in the political situation.

Israeli army chief of staff, Lieutenant General Amnon Shahak, joined Yaalon in saying that clashes between Israeli soldiers and Palestinian protesters at the weekend near Palestinian-ruled enclaves could have been stopped sooner by the Authority and had been encouraged by some of its officials.

"The clashes between the mob and our soldiers were led according to our information by the Fatah organisation...as far as we know encouraged by Jibril Rajoub himself and his apparatus," Yaalon said. Fatah is the mainstream PLO faction.

Asked to explain how Palestinian Preventive Security head Rajoub had a cordial meeting with Israeli Internal Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani on Sunday after encouraging riots, Shahak said: "Confusion is part of the process."
Shahak, asked if to defend itself Israel might retake West Bank cities it has handed to the Palestinians since signing a 1993 framework peace deal, said:
"I believe that all hope that this is not an option unless it will be necessary and I hope it will never be necessary."

Yaalon again repeated a charge, denied by the Authority, that Palestinian guerrilla groups had been given the impression they had a green light from the Palestinian Authority to commit attacks against Israel.

"In light of the situation, we estimate that as long as Arafat does not cause the terrorist organisations to understand that there is no green light to commit attacks, we are expecting more attacks," he said.
Hamas threatened to launch further attacks if Israel went on building a Jewish settlement begun last week in Arab East Jerusalem at Jabal Abu Ghneim, known as Har Homa in Israel.
The Israeli army said that it had arrested 37 Palestinians in the West Bank in sweeps spurred by the Tel Aviv bombing.

On Sunday Israeli security forces shot and wounded two Palestinians at a roadblock near Jerusalem and fired teargas to disperse Arab protesters who hurled five petrol bombs at them near the West Bank town of Hebron, witnesses said.
